turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your attempts at provocation are tiresome, Sandip. My concerns are not for my own safety, but for the well-being of those under my protection; and that includes my tenants, who deserve to live free from harassment of any kind.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Ah, 'well-being,' is it? A rather… lofty term, wouldn't you agree, Nikhil? One wonders if such benevolence extends to those who, perhaps, find themselves *disagreeing* with your methods, or questioning the very foundations upon which your ‘protection’ is built.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your insinuations are unproductive, Sandip. I find it increasingly difficult to discern whether you seek genuine discourse or merely to manufacture conflict. I suggest you reconsider the purpose of your visit.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Manufacture conflict, you say? A rather… pedestrian assessment, wouldn’t you agree, Nikhil? It seems you mistake my efforts at illumination for mere discord—a tragic misunderstanding, reminiscent, I daresay, of the tragic misunderstandings that plague the protagonists of Sophocles.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Sophocles… a curious reference, Sandip. Are you suggesting, then, that *we* are all characters in a predetermined tragedy?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Such literary comparisons are, I find, a distraction from the matter at hand. My concern remains the stability of this household and the security of those who depend on it, and I will not permit frivolous diversions to obscure that responsibility.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A predetermined tragedy, you say, Bimala? How delightfully pessimistic! But perhaps you grasp the essence of the situation more keenly than your husband allows himself to see – a certain… inevitability, wouldn’t you agree, Nikhil? The tides of influence, like the currents of the Ganges, are rarely steered by the whim of a single landowner.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: I confess, Sandip, the comparison is… arresting. But I am not so certain of any predetermined course; surely, even Sophocles allowed for a degree of human agency, however small. Perhaps it is not inevitability we face, but simply… shifting sands.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your insistence on drawing parallels to classical literature, Sandip, serves only to obfuscate the realities before us. I am not concerned with dramatic interpretations; I am concerned with demonstrable threats and the welfare of those under my protection. Let us return to the matter of the recent disturbances amongst my tenants.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Shifting sands, you say, Bimala? A rather poetic observation, though I daresay even the most picturesque dunes can conceal treacherous quicksand. Tell me, Nikhil, do you truly believe your walls of land and wealth can hold back a tide that originates not from the river, but from the very hearts of men?

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Quicksand is indeed a dangerous thing, Sandip, though I suspect its presence is not always so readily apparent. Perhaps we should all be mindful of what lies beneath the surface, wouldn’t you agree, Nikhil?

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Beneath the surface, you say, Bimala? How very perceptive. But tell me, do you perceive the subtle tremor, the barely perceptible shift in allegiance amongst those who toil for Nikhil? A loyalty bought with grain and comfort is a fragile thing, wouldn't you agree, easily swayed by… other persuasions?

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Allegiance is a complex thing, Sandip; it is not always readily quantifiable in terms of grain or comfort. Surely, even the most steadfast servant can experience a change of heart, influenced by factors beyond our immediate comprehension.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A change of heart, you say, Bimala? How eloquently put! But isn’t it often the case that such shifts are… *encouraged* by forces unseen, by whispers carried on the wind? I wonder, Nikhil, are you truly listening to the murmurs amongst your tenants, or are you too preoccupied with the rustling of your ledger to hear the rising tide of discontent?

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Murmurs can be deceiving, Sandip. Sometimes the wind carries only the echo of anxieties, not necessarily the prelude to a storm. I trust Nikhil is capable of discerning the difference.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Anxieties, you say? A charming euphemism, Bimala. But tell me, is a storm truly so terrible if it washes away the stagnant pools where discontent festers? Nikhil, I trust you’re not so sentimental as to cling to a system merely because it’s… *familiar*.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A storm, Sandip, can also destroy the fertile fields that nourish us. I find it rather unsettling how readily you equate discomfort with inherent injustice; surely, there is a middle ground to be sought, a path that avoids extremes.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Sandip, your rhetoric is unnecessary and unproductive. I am well aware of the concerns amongst my tenants, and I address them as I see fit, without the need for your dramatic pronouncements. My focus remains on ensuring stability and fairness, which includes preventing unnecessary agitation.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Stability, you say, Nikhil? A rather quaint aspiration, wouldn't you agree? One might even compare it to the Emperor Nero fiddling while Rome… well, you understand. I merely suggest that sometimes, a little instability is precisely what’s needed to clear the air, to expose the rot beneath the veneer of your precious 'fairness'.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your analogies, Sandip, are tiresome and reveal a fundamental misunderstanding of my purpose. I am not attempting to ignore discomfort, but to manage it responsibly, ensuring that solutions are grounded in reason and not fueled by inflammatory language. I trust you can appreciate the distinction.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I say, Nikhil, don't you keep Browning among your books here? I was just telling Queen Bee of our college club. Do you remember that contest of ours over the translation of those lines from Browning? You don't?

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I managed to get together the words to render it into Bengali, somehow, but the result was hardly likely to be a 'joy forever' to the people of Bengal. I really did think at one time that I was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence was kind enough to save me from that disaster. Do you remember old Dakshina? If he had not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet. I remember his rendering to this day ...

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: No, Queen Bee, it is no use rummaging those bookshelves. Nikhil has ceased to read poetry since his marriage--perhaps he has no further need for it. But I suppose 'the fever fit of poesy', as the Sanskrit has it, is about to attack me again.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I have come to give you a warning, Sandip.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: About the fever fit of poesy?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: For some time, Mahomedan preachers have been about stirring up the local Mussulmans. They are all wild with you, and may attack you any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Are you come to advise flight?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I have come to give you information, not to offer advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Had these estates been mine, such a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for me. If, instead of trying to frighten me, you give them a taste of your intimidation, that would be worthier both of you and me. Do you know that your weakness is weakening your neighbouring zamindars also?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I did not offer you my advice, Sandip. I wish you, too, would refrain from giving me yours. Besides, it is useless. And there is another thing I want to tell you. You and your followers have been secretly worrying and oppressing my tenantry. I cannot allow that any longer. So I must ask you to leave my territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: For fear of the Mussulmans, or is there any other fear you have to threaten me with?
